title: The hypertrophy series: volume vs tonnage
summary: First episode of the hypertrophy series, defining terms. Volume is sets x reps regardless of weight; tonnage is the total weight moved, and tonnage is what NH cares about most for growth. Hard sets are the bodybuilder's bread and butter, junk volume exists, and tonnage is best counted from working sets only, though warm-ups still matter. He uses 'tonnage' as a bodybuilding-specific term.

claims.claim: English is his third language, so he may use some established fitness terms in his own way.
Volume, as he uses it, is reps x sets in a session (e.g. 3x10 + 5x5 + 6x12) without considering weight; he seldom counts it.
Tonnage is the total weight moved (weight x reps summed), e.g. 200 lbs x 10 = 2000 lbs, and can be tracked daily, weekly, monthly or yearly.
He cares most about tonnage, but tonnage is created by volume; without volume there's no tonnage.
Tonnage alone is just a number that hides how the work was distributed; you need the volume breakdown into sets and reps to work within intensity windows.
What makes muscles grow is, and always will be, tonnage.
Hard sets are the bread and butter of a bodybuilder; junk volume exists that contributes little to hypertrophy. You can have ten hard sets in one workout across different planes.
Warm-ups matter: they aren't challenging enough to drive growth, but they prime you for heavier weight, so people who say they don't matter are wrong.
Calculating tonnage from working sets only, without warm-ups, better represents productive, quality work.
Talking only about per-session volume gives a false idea of the work done; tonnage is a fresher term that makes new lifters pay attention and lets you speak of productive tonnage.
YouTube fitness isn't bodybuilding-centric and natural bodybuilding is a fringe community; 'volume' is owned by powerlifting and weightlifting, so bodybuilding deserves its own term, tonnage.
